newsitem.title: USA: Liz Taylor celebrates 65th - week after brain surgery.
newsitem.headline: Liz Taylor celebrates 65th - week after brain surgery.

text.p: Two-time Oscar-winning actress Elizabeth Taylor was celebrating her 65th birthday quietly at home surrounded by her family on Thursday, just a week after undergoing delicate brain surgery.

There was no comment from the star as she was whisked into her Bel-Air estate in a Mercedes after leaving the hospital on Wednesday. Holding her white lap-dog, Taylor's head was swathed in a dark scarf to cover the scar from the operation in which surgeons drilled into her skull.

Announcing the screen legend had been discharged from the famed Cedars-Sinai Medical Centre, spokesman Ron Wise commented: "She has made an excellent recovery. The operation was a complete success and she should be able to resume her normal activities."
Taylor's publicist, Shirine Coburn, said the actress planned a quiet birthday celebration at home with family.

The violet-eyed star, who has been married eight times to seven husbands, widowed once and been through seven divorces, has four children and several grandchildren. Many of them had visited her during the eight days she was in the hospital.
Last Thursday she underwent four hours of surgery to remove an apparently benign tumour the size of a golf ball from the lining of her brain.

Dr. Martin Cooper, head of neurosurgery at Cedars-Sinai, said after the operation he expected full recovery. The tumour was a meningioma, about 2 inches (5 cm) across, and such tumours are always benign, he said.
The tumour, in the lining of her parietal lobe, just behind Taylor's left ear, was detected this month during a brain scan as part of a routine physical examination.

Thursday's quiet birthday celebration for the London-born actress was in stark contrast to the star-studded gala she attended two days before entering the hopsital. All Hollywood turned out for a glittering tribute at the Pantages Theatre to celebrate Taylor's birthday and her body of cinematic work.
The event, which was shown on ABC television last Tuesday, also raised over $1 million for AIDS research -- a cause dear to Taylor's heart since she stopped making movies.

Dressed in an emerald gown and dripping in diamond jewelry, she addressed the audience -- many of whom paid up to $1,000 per ticket. "I'm not here to celebrate my birthday. I'm here to celebrate all the people in the world with AIDS."

Taylor won the best actress Oscar in 1960 for her role as a call-girl in "Butterfield 8" and again in 1966 for her portrayal of an alcoholic wife opposite her own husband at the time, Richard Burton, in "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?"
But even her most acclaimed film roles have paled in comparison with a pain-filled reality. Taylor has been in and out of hospitals battling serious illness, injury and alcohol and drug dependency.

She has had two hip surgeries and was treated in 1995 for high blood pressure and an irregular heart beat. In 1990 she nearly died of viral pneumonia and had a relapse two years later that led to another hospital stay.
